Tutorial 3 - Climate Impact Analysis

Hurricane Wind Hazard Model for the Caribbean

2026-04-20

Source: vignettes/tutorial_3_climate_change.qmd

Prerequisites

This tutorial assumes you have already worked through Tutorial 1, where the single-site workflow and the main output objects are introduced in more detail.

This tutorial scales the workflow from a single site to a small group of islands, then compares a present-day baseline with a warmer climate. The aim is practical: run the model, inspect the annual output, and turn scenario differences into daily disruption metrics for one site.

1. What This Tutorial Covers

By the end, you will be able to:

  • run the baseline model for three islands at once;
  • compare today’s climate with a warmer scenario;
  • turn the annual scenario differences into day-by-day disruption metrics for one site.
library(ipdcstorm)
library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)

2. Multi-Site Baseline

We start with the three Dutch Caribbean islands used throughout the package: St. Martin, Saba, and Statia. The setup is the same as in Tutorial 1, only with three rows in targets instead of one.

seed <- 123L
simulation_years <- 500L

ibtracs_demo <- system.file(
  "extdata",
  "ibtracs_demo.csv",
  package = "ipdcstorm"
)

targets <- data.frame(
  name = c("St_Martin", "Saba", "Statia"),
  lat = c(18.0708, 17.6350, 17.4890),
  lon = c(-63.0501, -63.2300, -62.9740)
)

cfg_baseline <- make_hazard_cfg(
  data_path = ibtracs_demo,
  historical_start_year = 1970L,
  search_radius_km = 800,
  simulation_years = simulation_years,
  climate = make_climate_cfg(scenario = "stationary")
)
out_baseline <- run_hazard_model(
  cfg = cfg_baseline,
  targets = targets,
  seed = seed,
  verbose = FALSE
)

The rates table shows what the model learned from history: the average number of tropical-storm and hurricane hits per year at each island.

out_baseline$rates
#> # A tibble: 6 × 6
#>   location  storm_class lambda n_years prob_annual prob_none
#>   <chr>     <chr>        <dbl>   <int>       <dbl>     <dbl>
#> 1 St_Martin HUR          0.191      47       0.174     0.826
#> 2 St_Martin TS           0.553      47       0.425     0.575
#> 3 Saba      HUR          0.128      47       0.120     0.880
#> 4 Saba      TS           0.511      47       0.400     0.600
#> 5 Statia    HUR          0.149      47       0.138     0.862
#> 6 Statia    TS           0.511      47       0.400     0.600

The simulation table has one synthetic season per row. To compare islands at a glance, average the simulated counts and the hurricane share by location.

baseline_summary <- out_baseline$sim |>
  group_by(location) |>
  summarise(
    mean_total = mean(n_total, na.rm = TRUE),
    mean_ts = mean(n_ts, na.rm = TRUE),
    mean_hur = mean(n_hur, na.rm = TRUE),
    mean_p_hur = mean(p_hurricane, na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

baseline_summary
#> # A tibble: 3 × 5
#>   location  mean_total mean_ts mean_hur mean_p_hur
#>   <chr>          <dbl>   <dbl>    <dbl>      <dbl>
#> 1 Saba            1.19   1.02     0.17       0.141
#> 2 St_Martin       1.01   0.814    0.194      0.186
#> 3 Statia          1.25   1.09     0.16       0.137
Column Description
mean_total Average number of storms per year that hit the site at tropical-storm strength or above.
mean_ts Average number of tropical-storm events per year.
mean_hur Average number of hurricanes per year.
mean_p_hur Average share of events that reach hurricane strength.

These numbers should broadly match the rates table. Small differences between islands reflect real geography: some sites see storms pass close and strong more often than others.

3. Climate Change Scenarios

Warming affects the simulated climate in two ways. First, it can raise or lower the total number of storms per year (a rate effect). Second, it can shift the storm mix so a larger share reach hurricane strength (an intensity effect).

Both effects are driven by a single number: delta_sst, the change in Main Development Region sea-surface temperature (in °C) relative to a 1991-2020 baseline. You can either use a named scenario helper (IPCC AR6, KNMI’23) or set delta_sst directly.

Here we compare a stationary baseline (delta_sst = 0) with a warmer climate at delta_sst = 1.5. This side-by-side setup makes the direction and size of the climate response easy to see.

sst_scenario_info() |>
  filter(source == "ipcc_ar6") |>
  select(scenario, source, delta_sst_2050, delta_sst_2100)
#> # A tibble: 3 × 4
#>   scenario source   delta_sst_2050 delta_sst_2100
#>   <chr>    <chr>             <dbl>          <dbl>
#> 1 ssp126   ipcc_ar6            0.3            0.4
#> 2 ssp245   ipcc_ar6            0.5            1  
#> 3 ssp585   ipcc_ar6            1              2.5

The built-in scenario table is useful context, but for the tutorial we set delta_sst directly so the warming is visible in the code.

climate_future <- make_climate_cfg(
  delta_sst = 1.5,
  sensitivity_mode = "fixed"
)

cfg_future <- make_hazard_cfg(
  data_path = ibtracs_demo,
  historical_start_year = 1970L,
  search_radius_km = 800,
  simulation_years = simulation_years,
  climate = climate_future
)
out_future <- run_hazard_model(
  cfg = cfg_future,
  targets = targets,
  seed = seed,
  verbose = FALSE
)

Now stack the two simulation tables and compare by scenario and island. The summary reports the average yearly storm count, how it splits into tropical storms and hurricanes, and the simulated hurricane share.

activity_summary <- bind_rows(
  out_baseline$sim |> mutate(scenario = "Baseline"),
  out_future$sim |> mutate(scenario = "Future (+1.5 C)")
) |>
  group_by(scenario, location) |>
  summarise(
    mean_total = mean(n_total, na.rm = TRUE),
    mean_ts = mean(n_ts, na.rm = TRUE),
    mean_hur = mean(n_hur, na.rm = TRUE),
    mean_p_hur = mean(p_hurricane, na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) |>
  arrange(location, scenario)

activity_summary
#> # A tibble: 6 × 6
#>   scenario        location  mean_total mean_ts mean_hur mean_p_hur
#>   <chr>           <chr>          <dbl>   <dbl>    <dbl>      <dbl>
#> 1 Baseline        Saba            1.19   1.02     0.17       0.141
#> 2 Future (+1.5 C) Saba            1.24   1.03     0.204      0.168
#> 3 Baseline        St_Martin       1.01   0.814    0.194      0.186
#> 4 Future (+1.5 C) St_Martin       1.15   0.91     0.238      0.220
#> 5 Baseline        Statia          1.25   1.09     0.16       0.137
#> 6 Future (+1.5 C) Statia          1.31   1.11     0.202      0.162
Column Description
scenario Baseline or future — the label used in the comparison.
location Target island.
mean_total Average yearly storm count under that scenario.
mean_ts Average yearly tropical-storm count.
mean_hur Average yearly hurricane count.
mean_p_hur Average share of storms reaching hurricane strength. 
activity_summary |>
  ggplot(aes(x = location, y = mean_total, fill = scenario)) +
  geom_col(position = "dodge") +
  labs(
    x = NULL,
    y = "Mean annual storm count",
    fill = "Scenario",
    title = "Annual storm activity by scenario and location"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 11)

How to read scenario differences

Scenario differences describe the long-run average, not a forecast for any single year. A higher mean_total or mean_p_hur means the simulated climate is more active on average — but quiet years still happen.

4. Daily Series Comparison

Annual counts are useful for climatology, but many planning questions are about daily disruption. To show that step, we generate daily hazard and impact series for Saba under the baseline and the warmer scenario.

daily_baseline <- generate_daily_hazard_impact_spatial(
  out = out_baseline,
  location = "Saba",
  sim_years = 1:200,
  year0 = 2025,
  gust_factor = 1.25,
  damage = list(method = "intensity"),
  pulse_shape = "cosine",
  scenario = "Baseline",
  seed = 123
)$Saba

daily_future <- generate_daily_hazard_impact_spatial(
  out = out_future,
  location = "Saba",
  sim_years = 1:200,
  year0 = 2025,
  gust_factor = 1.25,
  damage = list(method = "intensity"),
  pulse_shape = "cosine",
  scenario = "Future (+1.5 C)",
  seed = 123
)$Saba

The combined table shows how often Saba experiences tropical-storm and hurricane days under each scenario, plus the average annual damage signal across the 200 simulated years.

daily_summary <- bind_rows(
  dplyr::mutate(daily_baseline, scenario = "Baseline"),
  dplyr::mutate(daily_future, scenario = "Future (+1.5 C)")
) |>
  group_by(scenario) |>
  summarise(
    tc_days = sum(wind_kt > 0, na.rm = TRUE),
    ts_days = sum(wind_kt >= 34, na.rm = TRUE),
    hur_days = sum(wind_kt >= 64, na.rm = TRUE),
    mean_annual_damage = sum(damage_rate, na.rm = TRUE) / 200,
    .groups = "drop"
  )

daily_summary
#> # A tibble: 2 × 5
#>   scenario        tc_days ts_days hur_days mean_annual_damage
#>   <chr>             <int>   <int>    <int>              <dbl>
#> 1 Baseline            840     408       81            0.00314
#> 2 Future (+1.5 C)     863     436       88            0.00291
daily_plot_data <- data.frame(
  scenario = rep(daily_summary$scenario, times = 3),
  metric = rep(
    c("TC days/year", "TS days/year", "HUR days/year"),
    each = nrow(daily_summary)
  ),
  value = c(
    daily_summary$tc_days / 200,
    daily_summary$ts_days / 200,
    daily_summary$hur_days / 200
  )
)

daily_plot_data |>
  ggplot(aes(x = metric, y = value, fill = scenario)) +
  geom_col(position = "dodge") +
  labs(
    x = NULL,
    y = "Mean annual days",
    fill = "Scenario",
    title = "Daily disruption metrics for Saba by scenario"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 11)
Column Description
tc_days Days where a storm produced any wind at the site (wind_kt > 0).
ts_days Days reaching at least 34 kt (tropical-storm strength).
hur_days Days reaching at least 64 kt (hurricane strength).
mean_annual_damage Average damage total per year across the 200 simulated seasons.

Adding trade-wind background to both scenarios

The daily series above have zero wind on every non-storm day. For applications that need a continuous wind record (wind energy, chronic exposure, port disruption), attach a make_background_wind_cfg() object to each hazard config. It then flows through to generate_daily_hazard_impact_spatial() automatically:

bg_cfg <- make_background_wind_cfg(
  weibull_params = list(
    Saba = tibble::tibble(month = 1:12, shape = 2.0, scale = 13)
  ),
  ar1 = 0.4
)

cfg_baseline_bg <- make_hazard_cfg(
  data_path = ibtracs_demo,
  historical_start_year = 1970L,
  simulation_years = simulation_years,
  climate = make_climate_cfg(scenario = "stationary"),
  background_wind = bg_cfg            # <-- attach once to each cfg
)

cfg_future_bg <- make_hazard_cfg(
  data_path = ibtracs_demo,
  historical_start_year = 1970L,
  simulation_years = simulation_years,
  climate = make_climate_cfg(delta_sst = 1.5, sensitivity_mode = "fixed"),
  background_wind = bg_cfg
)

After run_hazard_model(), call generate_daily_hazard_impact_spatial() without a background_wind argument — it picks the setting up from out$cfg$background_wind automatically, keeping the same seed so the climate comparison stays clean. See Tutorial 1 §Background Wind for guidance and a worked example.

About event-level perturbation

The package also supports event-level perturbation for more exploratory scenario analysis. We do not use it here, so the daily comparison isolates the rate and intensity effects discussed above.

5. Key Parameters

For most climate sensitivity runs, three settings matter most:

Parameter What it controls
delta_sst The warming (°C) relative to the 1991-2020 baseline. Here delta_sst = 1.5 sets the future climate directly.
scenario vs delta_sst Use a named scenario (e.g. IPCC AR6, KNMI’23) when you want to follow a published pathway. Use delta_sst when you want a transparent what-if value without committing to any specific pathway.
sensitivity_mode "fixed" keeps the calibrated climate sensitivities constant as warming grows. "linear_shifted" lets those sensitivities themselves vary with delta_sst — more exploratory.

Baseline-versus-scenario is a good starting point for stress-testing. Once the annual and daily outputs feel familiar, the same workflow scales to more islands or alternative warming assumptions.
